passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Protein T is a small, single-domain enzyme whose folded structure is rich in α helices. A biochemist compared four forms of the protein by thermal denaturation: wild-type (WT); a variant in which a buried leucine was replaced with alanine (L to A); a variant in which a surface lysine was replaced with glutamate (K to E); and a variant in which two residues on neighboring helices were each replaced with cysteine so that a disulfide bond could form (S-S). Each sample was held in identical buffer while the temperature was raised, and the circular dichroism (CD) signal at 222 nm, which reports on helical content, was converted to the fraction of protein folded. The melting temperature (Tm) is the temperature at which half of the protein is folded. Tm values are listed in Table 1, and the melting curves for WT and the S-S variant are shown in Figure 1.
Mass spectrometry confirmed that all four proteins had the expected masses, and the S-S variant was purified under oxidizing conditions so that its new disulfide bond was intact.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which variant would be mostly unfolded at 50 °C?
o: The L to A variant, because its Tm of 49 °C is below 50 °C
Correct: Its Tm of 49 °C is below 50 °C, so more than half of it is unfolded at 50 °C.
The WT protein, because it has the lowest Tm of the four forms
Not quite. WT has a Tm of 58 °C, higher than L to A, so it is mostly folded at 50 °C.
The K to E variant, because any charge reversal destabilizes a protein
Not quite. K to E has a Tm of 57 °C, almost the same as WT, so it is mostly folded at 50 °C.
The S-S variant, because covalent crosslinks make proteins rigid and prone to unfolding
Not quite. The S-S variant has the highest Tm (67 °C), so the crosslink stabilizes it.
qs.x: Correct: Tm is the melting temperature, the temperature where half of the protein is folded and half is unfolded. So at a temperature above its Tm, a protein is more than half unfolded. Table 1 lists four Tm values: WT 58 °C, L to A 49 °C, K to E 57 °C and S-S 67 °C. At 50 °C, the question is which variant has a Tm that has already been passed. Only L to A, at 49 °C, has, since 50 is above 49. The other three have Tm values above 50 °C, so more than half of each is still folded. Why the others are wrong: WT does not have the lowest Tm, since 58 is higher than 49, so it is still mostly folded at 50 °C; K to E has a Tm of 57 °C, almost the same as WT, so swapping a surface charge didn't destabilize it much; the S-S variant has the highest Tm in the table at 67 °C, because the disulfide crosslink stabilizes the fold. Trap: Guessing WT is the weakest because it sounds like the baseline, without reading the Tm column in Table 1.

qs.q: The higher Tm of the S-S variant is best explained by the disulfide bond:
o: restricting the conformations available to the unfolded chain, which raises the free-energy cost of unfolding
Correct: The crosslink limits the shapes the unfolded chain can take, so unfolding costs more and Tm rises.
adding a hydrophobic side chain to the core, which increases the entropy of the folded state
Not quite. A disulfide isn't a new hydrophobic core contact, and a more ordered folded state is not favored by higher entropy.
neutralizing the net charge of the protein so repulsion is removed
Not quite. A change in net charge doesn't explain a 9 °C rise in Tm.
converting α helices into β sheets, which resist heat
Not quite. The crosslink doesn't convert helices to sheets. The CD signal still reports helices.
qs.x: Correct: The S-S variant has two cysteines placed on neighboring helices (paragraph 1) that form a disulfide bond, a covalent link between them. Table 1 shows its Tm is 67 °C, versus 58 °C for WT, a 9 °C rise, and Figure 1 shows its curve shifted to higher temperature. Why does a crosslink help? When a protein unfolds, the chain gains a lot of freedom to move around (higher entropy). A disulfide ties two points together, so the unfolded chain has fewer shapes it can take. That means unfolding gains less entropy, so the cost of unfolding is higher. More heat energy is needed before the protein melts. Why the others are wrong: cysteines forming a disulfide aren't adding new hydrophobic contacts to the core, and higher entropy in a more ordered folded state would not help; neutralizing net charge doesn't explain a 9 °C rise; the crosslink doesn't turn α helices into β sheets, and the CD signal in paragraph 1 still reports helical content. Trap: Thinking only a stronger bond in the folded state explains the stability, and forgetting the entropy effect on the unfolded state.

qs.q: Replacing the surface lysine with glutamate changed Tm by only 1 °C, whereas replacing the buried leucine with alanine lowered it by 9 °C. Which explanation is most consistent with these results?
o: Surface residues never contribute to stability of any protein
Not quite. Surface residues can matter, as in salt bridges. This particular swap was just minor.
Leucine is polar and forms hydrogen bonds with water in the folded state
Not quite. Leucine is nonpolar and doesn't hydrogen bond with water.
The buried leucine contributes to hydrophobic packing in the core, which the smaller alanine side chain cannot fully provide
Correct: Buried leucine packs tightly in the core, and alanine is too small to fill that space, so stability drops.
Alanine is charged at physiological pH and is therefore poorly tolerated in the interior
Not quite. Alanine has a nonpolar methyl side chain and is uncharged at physiological pH.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows K to E has a Tm of 57 °C, only 1 °C below WT at 58 °C, and L to A has 49 °C, which is 9 °C lower (58 − 49 = 9). Paragraph 1 tells us the lysine was on the surface and the leucine was buried. Inside the folded protein, buried nonpolar side chains like leucine pack tightly against each other through hydrophobic and van der Waals contacts. Alanine has only a small methyl side chain, so swapping leucine for alanine leaves a gap (cavity) and weakens that packing, which lowers stability. A surface residue faces water and has fewer tight contacts, so swapping lysine for glutamate changes little. Why the others are wrong: saying surface residues never matter is too broad, because surface residues can form salt bridges, but this swap was minor; leucine is nonpolar and doesn't hydrogen bond with water; alanine is uncharged at physiological pH, with a nonpolar methyl side chain. Trap: Treating all substitutions as equal without asking whether the residue is buried or exposed.

qs.q: A loss of CD signal at 222 nm as the sample is heated mainly reflects loss of which structural feature?
o: Quaternary structure, through subunit dissociation
Not quite. Protein T is single-domain, so it has no subunit interface to lose.
Peptide bonds, through thermal hydrolysis
Not quite. Peptide bonds don't hydrolyze at these temperatures.
The amino acid sequence, through racemization
Not quite. The sequence isn't changed by this heating, and CD at 222 nm doesn't report on it.
α-helical secondary structure
Correct: The 222 nm signal reports helical backbone hydrogen bonding, which melts during denaturation.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says the CD signal at 222 nm reports helical content. Circular dichroism measures how a sample absorbs left- versus right-handed light. A coiled α-helix gives a strong signal near 222 nm because of its regular backbone hydrogen-bonding pattern. When heat breaks those hydrogen bonds, the helices melt, and the signal drops. That is why the authors turn the signal into the fraction folded in Figure 1. Why the others are wrong: protein T is single-domain, so there are no subunits to come apart (no quaternary structure to lose); peptide bonds don't break from heating at these temperatures, and mass spectrometry in paragraph 2 confirmed the expected masses; racemization is not what heating does here, and CD at 222 nm reports helical structure, not the amino acid sequence. Trap: Confusing denaturation (loss of higher-order structure) with breaking covalent bonds in the primary structure.

qs.q: Figure 1 shows that at 60 °C about 0.30 of WT and about 0.85 of the S-S variant are folded. The ratio of folded WT to folded S-S protein at 60 °C is closest to:
o: Not quite. WT has less folded protein than S-S at 60 °C, so the ratio is below 1.
Correct: 0.30 ÷ 0.85 is about 0.35, which is closest to 1 : 3.
Not quite. 1 : 10 would need a folded WT fraction of about 0.085.
Not quite. This flips the ratio. S-S has more folded protein at 60 °C.
qs.x: Correct: A ratio of WT to S-S means WT ÷ S-S, both as fractions folded. From Figure 1 at 60 °C, WT is 0.30 and S-S is 0.85. Ratio = 0.30 ÷ 0.85. To make the division easier, multiply top and bottom by 100: 30 ÷ 85. Divide both by 5: 6 ÷ 17, which is about 0.35. Now compare to the choices. 1 : 3 means 1 ÷ 3 = 0.33, which is the closest. It also makes sense in the curves, because WT is mostly unfolded by 60 °C (its Tm is 58 °C in Table 1), while S-S, with a Tm of 67 °C, is mostly folded. Why the others are wrong: 2 : 1 and 3 : 1 are both above 1, but WT has less folded protein than S-S at 60 °C, so the ratio must be below 1; 1 : 10 would need a folded WT fraction of about 0.085 (0.85 ÷ 10). Trap: Dividing in the wrong order and reporting the inverse ratio.

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: Three tripeptides were synthesized, each with a free amino terminus and a free carboxyl terminus: peptide 1 (Ala-Glu-Gly), peptide 2 (Lys-Ala-Gly), and peptide 3 (His-Ala-Ala). A researcher wanted to separate the peptides by charge. The isoelectric point (pI) of a peptide is the pH at which its net charge is zero. Approximate pKₐ values for the ionizable groups in short peptides are given in Table 1; assume that each group ionizes independently.

The peptides were first compared by paper electrophoresis in a buffer of pH 8.0. In a second experiment, a mixture of the three peptides was applied at pH 5.0 to a cation-exchange column, whose resin carries fixed negatively charged sulfonate groups. The column was washed with the starting buffer, and bound peptides were then eluted with a gradient of increasing NaCl concentration. Fractions were analyzed for peptide content by their absorbance after reaction with a reagent that detects free amino groups.

qs.q: The pI of peptide 1 is closest to:
o: Not quite. 5.6 averages the two termini and ignores the Glu side chain.
Correct: The neutral form lies between the carboxyl (3.1) and Glu (4.3) pKₐ values, so pI = 3.7.
Not quite. 6.1 averages Glu and the amino terminus, which bracket the −1 form, not the neutral form.
Not quite. 8.0 is the amino terminus pKₐ, not the neutral point of an acidic peptide.
qs.x: Correct: The pI is the pH where the peptide has zero net charge. Peptide 1 is Ala-Glu-Gly, with a free amino terminus and free carboxyl terminus (paragraph 1). Its ionizable groups from Table 1 are the carboxyl terminus (pKₐ 3.1), the Glu side chain (4.3) and the amino terminus (8.0). Go from low pH to high. At very low pH, nothing has lost a proton: amino +1, carboxyl 0, Glu 0, net +1. After pH 3.1 the carboxyl loses its proton (−1): net 0. After pH 4.3 the Glu side chain loses its proton: net −1. The neutral form exists between 3.1 and 4.3. So pI = (3.1 + 4.3) ÷ 2 = 7.4 ÷ 2 = 3.7. Why the others are wrong: 5.6 averages the two termini, (3.1 + 8.0) ÷ 2 = 5.55, and ignores Glu; 6.1 averages Glu and the amino terminus, (4.3 + 8.0) ÷ 2 = 6.15, but those two bracket the −1 form, not the neutral form; 8.0 is just the amino terminus pKₐ. Trap: Using only the two terminal groups and ignoring the acidic Glu side chain.

qs.q: At pH 7.0, the net charge of peptide 2 is closest to:
o: Not quite. 0 would need the amino terminus and Lys to be neutral, but both are still protonated at pH 7.0.
Correct: Lys +1, amino terminus about +0.9 and carboxyl −1 add up to about +1.
Not quite. −1 would need Lys and the amino group to be neutral, which happens only far above pH 10.
Not quite. +2 ignores the negative charge on the ionized carboxyl terminus.
qs.x: Correct: Peptide 2 is Lys-Ala-Gly, with groups from Table 1: carboxyl terminus (pKₐ 3.1), amino terminus (8.0) and Lys side chain (10.5). At pH 7.0, a group is mostly protonated if pH is below its pKₐ and mostly deprotonated if above. Carboxyl terminus: pH 7.0 is above 3.1, so it has lost its proton and is −1. Lys side chain: 7.0 is below 10.5, so it is protonated, +1. Amino terminus: 7.0 is below 8.0, so it is mostly protonated, about +0.9 (a full +1 would be 100%, and at 1 pH unit below the pKₐ it's about 90% protonated). Add: −1 + 1 + 0.9 = +0.9, which is closest to +1. Why the others are wrong: 0 would need both the amino terminus and Lys to be neutral, but both are still protonated at pH 7.0; −1 would need both of them to be neutral too, which only happens far above pH 10; +2 counts both positives as full and ignores the negative carboxyl terminus. Trap: Counting the two positive groups and forgetting to subtract the carboxylate.

qs.q: In paper electrophoresis at pH 8.0, peptide 3 (pI 7.0) will most likely:
o: migrate toward the anode, because pH 8.0 is above its pI and it carries a net negative charge
Correct: pH 8.0 is above the pI of 7.0, so the peptide is net negative and moves toward the anode.
remain at the origin, because any pH above 7 gives zero net charge
Not quite. Zero net charge occurs only at the pI of 7.0, not at all higher pH values.
migrate toward the cathode, because pH 8.0 is above its pI
Not quite. Above the pI the charge is negative, so it moves toward the anode, not the cathode.
migrate toward the cathode, because its His side chain is protonated at pH 8.0
Not quite. His (pKₐ 6.0) is mostly deprotonated at pH 8.0 and doesn't give a net positive charge.
qs.x: Correct: Electrophoresis moves charged molecules in an electric field. A negative peptide goes toward the positive electrode (the anode), and a positive one goes toward the negative electrode (the cathode). The pI is the pH of zero net charge. Above the pI the peptide has lost more protons, so it is net negative. Peptide 3 (His-Ala-Ala) has a pI of 7.0, and the buffer in paragraph 2 is pH 8.0. Since 8.0 is above 7.0, peptide 3 is net negative and moves toward the anode. Why the others are wrong: staying at the origin would happen only at pH 7.0, its pI, not at every pH above 7; moving toward the cathode because pH 8.0 is above the pI has the logic backwards, since above the pI the charge is negative; moving toward the cathode because His is protonated fails, since His (pKₐ 6.0) is mostly deprotonated at pH 8.0 and does not give a net positive charge. Trap: Getting the direction of migration wrong relative to the pI. Above the pI, the peptide goes to the anode.

qs.q: In the cation-exchange experiment at pH 5.0, which peptide will pass through the column without binding?
o: Peptide 1
Correct: Peptide 1 is net negative at pH 5.0, so the negative resin repels it and it passes through.
All three peptides bind, because the resin binds every polypeptide at any pH
Not quite. Binding depends on net charge, and a net negative peptide isn't retained.
Peptide 3
Not quite. Peptide 3 is about +1 at pH 5.0, so it binds the resin.
Peptide 2
Not quite. Peptide 2 is +1 at pH 5.0, so it binds the sulfonate resin.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says the column is a cation exchanger, whose resin carries fixed negative sulfonate groups. It binds positively charged molecules (cations) and lets negative ones pass. So find the peptide that is not positive at pH 5.0. Peptide 1 (Ala-Glu-Gly): amino terminus (pKₐ 8.0) is protonated, +1; carboxyl terminus (3.1) and Glu side chain (4.3) are both below pH 5.0, so both have lost protons, −1 and about −0.8. Net is about −0.8, close to −1, negative, so it passes through. Peptide 2 and peptide 3 are each net positive at pH 5.0 and bind. Why the others are wrong: saying all three bind ignores that binding depends on net charge; peptide 3 (His-Ala-Ala) is about +1 (amino terminus +1, His mostly protonated since 5.0 is below 6.0, carboxyl −1); peptide 2 (Lys-Ala-Gly) is about +1 (amino +1, Lys +1, carboxyl −1). Trap: Forgetting that a cation exchanger holds positive molecules and lets negative ones pass.

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: Two membrane receptors, R1 and R2, bind the same soluble ligand L. The extracellular domain of each receptor was immobilized on a sensor chip, and ligand at several concentrations was passed over the surface in a surface plasmon resonance (SPR) experiment. Binding was followed in real time to obtain the association rate constant (kon) and the dissociation rate constant (koff) for each receptor, and the fraction of receptor sites occupied at equilibrium (Y) was recorded at each ligand concentration. For simple one-to-one binding, the dissociation constant is Kd = koff/kon, and Y = [L]/(Kd + [L]).

Selected values are given in Table 1, and the full equilibrium binding curves are plotted in Figure 1. The ligand concentration range used in the experiment was chosen to span the Kd values of both receptors. After equilibrium measurements, buffer without ligand was flowed over the chip so that the decay of the bound signal could be followed.

qs.q: Which conclusion about the two receptors is best supported by Table 1 and Figure 1?
o: R2 binds L with higher affinity, because it requires more ligand to saturate
Not quite. Needing more ligand to bind means lower affinity, not higher.
The receptors have equal affinity, because kon is identical
Not quite. Affinity depends on koff ÷ kon, and koff differs 10-fold.
R2 binds L with higher affinity, because its koff is larger
Not quite. A larger koff means faster release, which lowers affinity.
R1 binds L with higher affinity, because it reaches half-saturation at a lower ligand concentration
Correct: R1 is half-saturated at 10 nM and R2 at 100 nM, so R1 has the lower Kd and higher affinity.
qs.x: Correct: Affinity is how tightly a receptor holds its ligand. The lower the Kd (dissociation constant), the tighter the binding. A simple way to read Kd from the curves is that it equals the ligand concentration where Y (fraction of sites occupied) is 0.50. Table 1 shows R1 hits Y = 0.50 at 10 nM ligand, while R2 has Y = 0.50 only at 100 nM. Figure 1 agrees, with the R1 curve sitting to the left of R2. So R1 needs less ligand to be half full, which means a lower Kd and higher affinity. Why the others are wrong: needing more ligand to saturate means lower affinity, so R2 is the weaker binder; equal kon doesn't mean equal affinity, because Kd = koff ÷ kon and the koff values differ 10-fold (0.010 versus 0.10); a larger koff means the ligand leaves faster, which lowers affinity. Trap: Equating a larger koff, or a need for more ligand, with tighter binding.

qs.q: What is the Kd of receptor R2 for ligand L?
o: 100 nM
0.1 nM
Not quite. This comes from inverting the ratio and mis-scaling the exponent.
1 µM
Not quite. 1 μM would need a koff of 1.0 s⁻¹.
10 nM
Not quite. 10 nM is the Kd of R1, not R2.
qs.x: Correct: The formula is Kd = koff ÷ kon, as given in paragraph 1. For R2, Table 1 gives koff = 0.10 s⁻¹ and kon = 1 × 10⁶ M⁻¹ s⁻¹. Plug in: Kd = 0.10 ÷ (1 × 10⁶). Write 0.10 as 1 × 10⁻¹. Dividing powers of 10, subtract the exponents: −1 − 6 = −7. So Kd = 1 × 10⁻⁷ M. Now convert to nM. 1 nM = 10⁻⁹ M, so divide by 10⁻⁹ (subtract the exponent: −7 − (−9) = −7 + 9 = 2). That gives 1 × 10² nM = 100 nM. This matches Table 1, where R2 is half full (Y = 0.50) at 100 nM. Why the others are wrong: 0.1 nM comes from inverting the ratio and slipping on the exponent; 1 μM (1,000 nM) would need a koff of 1.0 s⁻¹; 10 nM is the Kd of R1 (0.010 ÷ 1 × 10⁶ = 1 × 10⁻⁸ M). Trap: Using kon ÷ koff instead of koff ÷ kon, or slipping a power of 10 when converting to nM.

qs.q: The difference in affinity between R1 and R2 is primarily due to a difference in:
o: the molecular mass of the ligand bound
Not quite. Both receptors bind the same ligand.
how rapidly ligand and receptor associate
Not quite. kon is the same for both receptors.
the total number of receptor sites on the chip
Not quite. Y is a fraction, so it doesn't depend on the number of sites.
the rate of complex dissociation
Correct: kon is equal, so the 10-fold Kd difference comes from the 10-fold difference in koff.
qs.x: Correct: Kd = koff ÷ kon. Table 1 shows both receptors have the same kon, 1 × 10⁶ M⁻¹ s⁻¹. Their koff values are 0.010 s⁻¹ for R1 and 0.10 s⁻¹ for R2. Since 0.10 ÷ 0.010 = 10, R2 lets go of the ligand 10 times faster. With kon equal, the Kd of R2 is 10 times bigger than the Kd of R1 (100 nM versus 10 nM). So the affinity difference comes entirely from how fast the complex falls apart. Why the others are wrong: both receptors bind the same ligand L (paragraph 1), so its mass is the same; association speed is the same, because kon is identical; Y is a fraction of sites occupied, so it doesn't depend on how many sites are on the chip. Trap: Assuming tighter binding must come from faster association instead of slower dissociation.

qs.q: Assuming first-order dissociation, the half-life of the R1-L complex after ligand removal is closest to:
o: Correct: t½ = ln 2 ÷ koff = 0.693 ÷ 0.010 s⁻¹ ≈ 69 s.
Not quite. 100 s is 1 ÷ koff, the mean lifetime, not the half-life.
Not quite. 6.9 s would use koff = 0.10 s⁻¹, which is R2's value.
Not quite. 0.69 s mis-scales the exponent when dividing.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says buffer without ligand was flowed over the chip so the bound signal decays. For first-order decay, the half-life is t½ = ln 2 ÷ koff, where t½ is the time for half the complex to fall apart. R1's koff from Table 1 is 0.010 s⁻¹. ln 2 is about 0.693. Plug in: t½ = 0.693 ÷ 0.010 s⁻¹. Dividing by 0.010 is the same as multiplying by 100: 0.693 × 100 = 69.3 s, so about 69 s. Why the others are wrong: 100 s is 1 ÷ koff = 1 ÷ 0.010 = 100 s, which is the mean lifetime, not the half-life; 6.9 s would come from koff = 0.10 s⁻¹, which is the R2 value (0.693 ÷ 0.10 = 6.93); 0.69 s mis-scales the exponent, as if koff were 1 s⁻¹. Trap: Reporting 1 ÷ koff (100 s) instead of ln 2 ÷ koff.

qs.q: At 10 nM ligand, the fraction of R1 sites occupied compared with the fraction of R2 sites occupied is about:
o: 5 times higher
Correct: 0.50 ÷ 0.09 is about 5.6, so R1 is about five times more occupied than R2.
10 times higher
Not quite. The 10-fold difference is in Kd, but occupancy isn't simply proportional to Kd.
the same
Not quite. The receptors have different Kd values, so their occupancy differs.
2 times lower
Not quite. R1 has the lower Kd and is more occupied, not less.
qs.x: Correct: Read Y at 10 nM from Table 1 (or Figure 1). R1 is 0.50 and R2 is 0.09. Check with Y = [L] ÷ (Kd + [L]): for R1, Kd = 10 nM, so Y = 10 ÷ (10 + 10) = 0.50; for R2, Kd = 100 nM, so Y = 10 ÷ (100 + 10) = 10 ÷ 110 = 0.09. Compare: 0.50 ÷ 0.09 = 5.6, so R1 is about 5 times more occupied than R2. Why the others are wrong: 10 times higher is the Kd ratio (100 ÷ 10), but occupancy isn't proportional to Kd, since R1 is already getting close to saturation; the same is wrong because their Kd values differ, so occupancy differs; 2 times lower flips things, because R1 has the lower Kd and is more occupied, not less. Trap: Assuming occupancy differs by exactly the ratio of the Kd values.

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Plasmid pTX is a circular, double-stranded DNA molecule of 6.0 kb that carries an ampicillin-resistance gene. A student digested samples of pTX with the restriction enzymes EcoRI, BamHI, and HindIII, alone and in combination, and separated the products by agarose gel electrophoresis. Fragment sizes were estimated by comparison with a DNA size ladder; they are listed in Table 1. EcoRI recognizes the palindromic sequence GAATTC and cuts between G and A on each strand, leaving single-stranded 5' overhangs.

The student then purified a 1.2 kb DNA fragment that had EcoRI-cut ends and no internal EcoRI site. The fragment was mixed with EcoRI-linearized pTX in the presence of DNA ligase and ATP, and the mixture was used to transform E. coli, which were plated on medium containing ampicillin. Colonies were picked, plasmid DNA was prepared, and each preparation was digested with EcoRI to confirm the presence of the insert. The digestion products were then compared with the pattern expected for the original plasmid on the same gel.

qs.q: How many HindIII recognition sites are present in pTX?
o: One
Not quite. One cut gives one linear 6.0 kb fragment, as EcoRI does.
Four
Not quite. Four sites would give four fragments in a circular plasmid.
Two
Correct: A circular plasmid cut at n sites gives n fragments, and HindIII gives two.
Three
Not quite. Three sites would give three fragments.
qs.x: Correct: pTX is a circular plasmid (paragraph 1). A circle has no ends. Each cut opens it up. One cut turns the circle into one straight piece. Two cuts give two pieces. In general, a circular DNA cut at n sites gives n fragments. Table 1 shows HindIII gives two fragments, 4.0 and 2.0 kb (which add up to 6.0 kb, the full plasmid). So there are two HindIII sites. Why the others are wrong: one site would give a single 6.0 kb linear piece, as EcoRI does in Table 1; three sites would give three fragments; four sites would give four fragments. Trap: Using the rule for linear DNA (fragments = sites + 1) on a circular plasmid, where fragments = sites.

qs.q: The data in Table 1 indicate that the EcoRI site lies:
o: within the 1.5 kb BamHI fragment and the 4.0 kb HindIII fragment
Not quite. The 1.5 kb BamHI fragment is unchanged in the double digest, so EcoRI doesn't cut it.
within the 1.5 kb BamHI fragment and the 2.0 kb HindIII fragment
Not quite. The 1.5 kb BamHI fragment stays whole in the EcoRI + BamHI digest.
in the 4.5 kb BamHI and 2.0 kb HindIII fragments
Correct: EcoRI splits 4.5 kb into 3.5 + 1.0 and 2.0 kb into 1.5 + 0.5, so it lies in both of those fragments.
exactly at one of the two BamHI recognition sites in the plasmid
Not quite. A cut at a BamHI site wouldn't make the 3.5 and 1.0 kb fragments.
qs.x: Correct: Compare the single digests to the double digests in Table 1. BamHI alone gives 4.5 and 1.5 kb. EcoRI + BamHI gives 3.5, 1.5 and 1.0 kb. The 1.5 kb piece is still there, and the 4.5 kb piece has been replaced by 3.5 + 1.0 (3.5 + 1.0 = 4.5). So EcoRI cuts inside the 4.5 kb BamHI fragment. HindIII alone gives 4.0 and 2.0 kb. EcoRI + HindIII gives 4.0, 1.5 and 0.5 kb. The 4.0 kb piece is still there, and the 2.0 kb piece has become 1.5 + 0.5 (1.5 + 0.5 = 2.0). So the single EcoRI site (EcoRI alone gives one 6.0 kb piece) lies in both the 4.5 kb BamHI fragment and the 2.0 kb HindIII fragment. Why the others are wrong: the 1.5 kb BamHI fragment is unchanged in the double digest, so EcoRI doesn't cut it, and the 4.0 kb HindIII fragment is also unchanged; a cut exactly at a BamHI site would leave 4.5 kb intact, and it wouldn't produce 3.5 and 1.0. Trap: Looking at the fragment that got smaller instead of the one that was actually split.

qs.q: Digestion of a recombinant plasmid containing one copy of the 1.2 kb insert with EcoRI is expected to yield:
o: a single linear fragment of 7.2 kb
Not quite. A single 7.2 kb piece would need the joints not to be recut, but EcoRI recognizes them again.
fragments of 6.0 kb and 1.2 kb, regardless of the orientation of the insert
Correct: Both joints regenerate EcoRI sites, so cutting releases the 6.0 kb vector and the 1.2 kb insert in either orientation.
fragments of 4.8 kb and 1.2 kb
Not quite. The vector is 6.0 kb, and the insert doesn't get subtracted from it.
fragments of 6.0 kb and 1.2 kb only if the insert is in a single orientation
Not quite. Either orientation regenerates the same EcoRI sites.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says the insert has EcoRI-cut ends and the vector was cut with EcoRI, then they were joined by ligase. At each of the two joints, the GAATTC sequence is rebuilt, because the sticky ends match up and the sequence on both sides is the same as before. EcoRI can cut at both joints again. Cutting there releases the insert (1.2 kb) and the vector (6.0 kb, the size of the original plasmid in Table 1). The insert can go in either direction, and both ways make the same two EcoRI sites, so the digest looks the same. Why the others are wrong: a single 7.2 kb piece (6.0 + 1.2 = 7.2) would mean the joints are not recut, but they are; 4.8 kb is 6.0 − 1.2, which wrongly subtracts the insert from the vector; claiming the pattern depends on a single orientation is wrong, because either orientation gives the same two EcoRI sites. Trap: Adding the sizes and expecting a single 7.2 kb fragment, forgetting that the joints are recut by EcoRI.

qs.q: In the EcoRI + BamHI digest, which fragment will migrate farthest through the gel toward the positive electrode?
o: The 1.5 kb fragment
Not quite. The 1.5 kb fragment is larger than 1.0 kb, so it travels a shorter distance.
All fragments move equally, because charge per base is constant
Not quite. The gel sorts by length, so the fragments migrate different distances.
The 1.0 kb fragment
Correct: The 1.0 kb fragment is the shortest, so it moves through the agarose most easily and travels farthest.
The 3.5 kb fragment
Not quite. The 3.5 kb fragment is the largest and migrates the least.
qs.x: Correct: In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate backbone, so it moves toward the positive electrode. The gel is like a mesh. Short fragments wiggle through easily and travel far. Long fragments get snagged and travel less. In the EcoRI + BamHI digest, Table 1 lists three fragments: 3.5, 1.5 and 1.0 kb. The shortest one, 1.0 kb, runs farthest. Why the others are wrong: the 1.5 kb fragment is bigger than 1.0 kb, so it moves a shorter distance; saying all move equally is wrong, because although charge per base is nearly constant, the gel sorts by length, so mobility differs; the 3.5 kb fragment is the largest, so it travels the least. Trap: Thinking equal charge per base means equal mobility.

qs.q: Digesting both the insert and the vector with EcoRI before adding ligase is useful because:
o: EcoRI methylates the ends, so the two DNAs recombine without ligase
Not quite. EcoRI cuts DNA. It doesn't methylate or join it.
EcoRI converts both fragments to single-stranded DNA
Not quite. EcoRI leaves double-stranded DNA with short overhangs, not fully single strands.
the complementary single-stranded overhangs on the two molecules can base-pair, and ligase then seals the sugar-phosphate backbone
Correct: Matching sticky ends anneal, and ligase then seals the backbone with phosphodiester bonds.
EcoRI removes the origin of replication from both fragments
Not quite. A single cut doesn't remove the origin, which the plasmid needs to replicate.
qs.x: Correct: EcoRI cuts GAATTC between G and A on each strand, which leaves short single-stranded overhangs (paragraph 1), called sticky ends. When the insert and the vector are both cut with EcoRI, their overhangs are complementary and can pair with each other by hydrogen bonds. That holds the pieces together side by side. Ligase then seals the gaps by making phosphodiester bonds between the 3′-OH and the 5′-phosphate, joining the sugar-phosphate backbone (paragraph 2). Why the others are wrong: EcoRI is a nuclease that cuts DNA, and it does not methylate or join it; EcoRI leaves double-stranded DNA with short overhangs, not fully single-stranded DNA; cutting at a single site doesn't remove the origin of replication, and the recombinant plasmid needs it to replicate. Trap: Believing the restriction enzyme itself joins the pieces, when it only makes compatible ends for ligase.

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: Researchers treated cultured cells with compound C, which activates a transcription factor, and measured changes in the abundance of two messenger RNAs by reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Total RNA was extracted after 8 hours of treatment with compound C or with vehicle alone, equal amounts of RNA were converted to complementary DNA, and gene G, gene H, and a reference gene were each amplified. The cycle threshold (Ct) is the PCR cycle at which fluorescence first exceeds a set threshold; a lower Ct means more starting template. The reference gene is expressed at a constant level in these cells. Assuming that each amplification doubles the product every cycle, relative expression is calculated as 2 raised to the power of minus the difference between the treated and vehicle values of (Ct target minus Ct reference).
Results at 8 hours are shown in Table 1. In a separate time course, the fold change in gene G mRNA relative to time zero was measured (Figure 1).

qs.q: Based on Table 1, treatment with compound C changed the abundance of gene G mRNA by:
o: an 8-fold decrease
Not quite. A lower Ct means more template, so the mRNA increased.
a 3-fold increase
Not quite. 3 is the Ct difference, but the fold change is 2³ because each cycle doubles.
a 6-fold increase
Not quite. This adds the Ct differences (3 + 3) instead of raising 2 to the difference.
an 8-fold increase
Correct: The target Ct fell by 3 cycles with the reference unchanged, so abundance rose 2³ = 8-fold.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 gives the formula: relative expression = 2 raised to the power of −[(Ct target − Ct reference) in treated − (Ct target − Ct reference) in vehicle]. Read the values for gene G from Table 1. Vehicle: Ct target = 24, Ct reference = 18. Treated: Ct target = 21, Ct reference = 18. Vehicle difference: 24 − 18 = 6. Treated difference: 21 − 18 = 3. Treated minus vehicle: 3 − 6 = −3. Plug in: relative expression = 2 raised to the power of −(−3). Two minus signs cancel, so this is 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Gene G rose 8-fold. This also fits: the target Ct dropped by 3 cycles, and since a lower Ct means more starting template, there was more mRNA. Each cycle is a doubling, so 3 cycles is 2³. Why the others are wrong: an 8-fold decrease flips the direction, because a lower Ct means more template; 3-fold uses the Ct difference as the fold change without raising 2 to it; 6-fold adds 3 + 3 instead of using the power of 2. Trap: Reporting the Ct difference as the fold change instead of 2 raised to that difference.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, the relative expression of gene H after compound C treatment is:
o: unchanged, because the reference gene Ct did not change
Not quite. The target Ct went from 26 to 29 while the reference stayed at 18, so expression changed.
0.33 of the vehicle level
Not quite. 0.33 is 1/3, taken from the Ct difference instead of 2⁻³.
1/8 of the vehicle level
Correct: The target Ct rose by 3 cycles, so relative expression is 2⁻³ = 1/8 = 0.125.
8 times the vehicle level
Not quite. A higher Ct means less template, so expression went down.
qs.x: Correct: Use the formula in paragraph 1: relative expression = 2 raised to the power of −(treated difference − vehicle difference), where each difference is Ct target − Ct reference. Gene H in Table 1: vehicle Ct target = 26, reference = 18, so the difference is 26 − 18 = 8. Treated Ct target = 29, reference = 18, so the difference is 29 − 18 = 11. Treated minus vehicle: 11 − 8 = 3. Plug in: relative expression = 2 raised to the power of −3. A negative exponent means one over: 2⁻³ = 1 ÷ 2³ = 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125. So gene H fell to 1/8 of the vehicle level. A higher Ct (29 versus 26) means it took 3 more cycles to see the signal, so there was less starting mRNA. Why the others are wrong: unchanged ignores that the target Ct moved from 26 to 29 while the reference stayed at 18; 0.33 takes 1/3 from the Ct difference rather than 2⁻³; 8 times higher flips the direction, because a higher Ct means less template. Trap: Reading a higher Ct as higher expression.

qs.q: The reference gene is included in each RT-qPCR reaction primarily to:
o: amplify the target gene to a higher final yield
Not quite. The reference gene is amplified separately and doesn't boost the target.
confirm that compound C enters the cells
Not quite. A constant reference gene says nothing about drug uptake.
correct for differences in the amount of RNA and the efficiency of cDNA synthesis among samples
Correct: A constantly expressed reference corrects for differences in RNA amount and cDNA or PCR efficiency between samples.
act as a primer for reverse transcriptase
Not quite. Primers are short oligonucleotides. The reference gene is a measured target.
qs.x: Correct: In paragraph 1, the reference gene is described as expressed at a constant level in these cells. Different tubes won't have exactly the same amount of RNA, and the cDNA step and PCR may work a little better in one tube than another. Since the reference gene should be the same in every sample, any difference in its Ct tells you the tubes weren't equal. In the formula, each target Ct is compared to the reference Ct from the same sample, which cancels out these differences. What is left is a real change in the target gene. Why the others are wrong: the reference gene is amplified on its own and doesn't boost the target's signal; a constant reference gene says nothing about whether compound C got into the cells; a primer is a short piece of DNA that starts copying, and the reference gene is a measured target, not a primer. Trap: Thinking the reference is a positive control for treatment instead of a tool to normalize.

qs.q: RNA is first converted to cDNA in this procedure because:
o: PCR polymerase needs a DNA template
Correct: PCR polymerase copies only DNA, so reverse transcriptase first makes cDNA from the mRNA.
mRNA cannot be quantified by fluorescence of any kind
Not quite. Fluorescence isn't the issue. The assay needs a DNA template for PCR.
DNA polymerase cannot function above 37 °C unless RNA is removed
Not quite. PCR polymerase is thermostable, and RNA isn't what limits it.
RNA does not contain the genetic information of the gene
Not quite. mRNA carries the gene's sequence and is the starting point of the assay.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says total RNA was converted to complementary DNA (cDNA) before PCR. The reason is that the DNA polymerase used in PCR only copies a DNA template. It can't copy RNA. The enzyme reverse transcriptase reads the mRNA and makes a matching strand of DNA (cDNA). Then PCR can amplify the cDNA, doubling it each cycle, which is how the Ct values in Table 1 come about. Why the others are wrong: RNA can be quantified by fluorescence in some methods, so the issue isn't RNA detection but the template requirement of PCR; the polymerase used in PCR is heat-stable (it survives high temperatures), and RNA isn't what limits it; mRNA does contain the genetic information of the gene, since it is a copy of the gene's sequence. Trap: Assuming RNA can't be amplified because it has no sequence information.

qs.q: The plateau in gene G mRNA between 8 and 24 hours (Figure 1) is most consistent with:
o: transcription of gene G having stopped completely at 8 hours
Not quite. If transcription stopped, mRNA would decline as it degraded.
degradation of gene G mRNA having stopped at 8 hours
Not quite. If degradation stopped while synthesis went on, the level would keep rising.
compound C having been fully metabolized by 8 hours
Not quite. Losing the drug would lower the mRNA, not hold it at 8-fold.
synthesis and degradation having balanced
Correct: A flat level means mRNA production and decay are balanced, even though both continue.
qs.x: Correct: Figure 1 shows gene G mRNA rising from 1 at time 0 to 2.5 at 2 h, 5 at 4 h and 8 at 8 h, then staying at 8 at 24 h. mRNA level depends on two things happening all the time: new mRNA being made (transcription) and old mRNA being broken down (degradation). When the two are equal, the level stays flat even though both are still going. That is a steady state. So the plateau is best explained by synthesis and degradation having balanced. Why the others are wrong: if transcription fully stopped, mRNA would fall as it degraded, not hold flat; if degradation stopped but synthesis continued, the level would keep climbing; if compound C were used up by 8 hours, the mRNA would drop back toward 1, not stay at 8. Trap: Reading a flat curve as meaning everything has stopped, when it can mean two opposing rates are equal.

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: To dissect the regulation of a human gene, PRM1, researchers cloned its upstream region into a plasmid placed in front of a firefly luciferase reporter gene. The full-length construct contained a TATA box located 30 bp upstream of the transcription start site and an enhancer element located 1,200 bp upstream. Additional constructs lacked the enhancer, lacked the TATA box, carried the enhancer in the reverse orientation, or carried the enhancer relocated 3 kb downstream of the reporter gene. Each plasmid was transfected into cultured cells together with a second plasmid that constitutively expresses Renilla luciferase. After 24 hours, firefly luciferase activity was divided by Renilla luciferase activity, and the ratio for the full-length construct was set to 100. Results are shown in Table 1.

The enhancer sequence was found to bind an activating transcription factor that is present in the transfected cell type. Cells were grown under identical conditions, and every construct was tested in triplicate on the same day.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the drop in activity from 100 to 12 when the enhancer is deleted?
o: The enhancer encodes part of the luciferase protein
Not quite. Enhancers are regulatory DNA, not coding sequence for the reporter.
The enhancer contributes positively to transcription of the reporter gene
Correct: Removing an activator-binding element lowers expression, so the enhancer normally boosts transcription.
The enhancer represses transcription by binding a repressor
Not quite. Removing a repressor site would raise expression, not lower it.
The enhancer is an essential part of the core promoter that RNA polymerase II requires to start
Not quite. Activity of 12 shows transcription can occur without it, so it isn't an essential core element.
qs.x: Correct: The full-length construct was set to 100 (paragraph 1). Table 1 shows that deleting the enhancer drops activity to 12. So taking the enhancer out lowers transcription of the reporter. Paragraph 2 says the enhancer binds an activating transcription factor. An enhancer is a stretch of DNA that, when an activator binds it, boosts transcription of a nearby gene. So the drop shows the enhancer normally boosts transcription. Why the others are wrong: an enhancer is a regulatory DNA sequence, not coding sequence, so it doesn't make part of the luciferase protein; if it bound a repressor, removing it would raise expression, not lower it; the enhancer isn't an essential core promoter part, because activity of 12 shows transcription still occurs without it, while deleting an essential element like the TATA box drops activity to 3. Trap: Confusing an enhancer, which turns transcription up, with a core promoter element, which is needed for any transcription.

qs.q: The results for the reverse-orientation and relocated enhancer constructs show that, in this system, the enhancer:
o: is converted to a promoter when moved
Not quite. Moving it doesn't give a TATA box, and activity stays about the same.
works in any orientation or place
Correct: Activity stays near 95 and 90 after inversion and relocation, as expected for an enhancer.
works only when positioned upstream and in the forward orientation
Not quite. Activity of 95 and 90 in the other configurations contradicts this.
must be adjacent to the TATA box to function
Not quite. It works from 1,200 bp upstream and from 3 kb downstream.
qs.x: Correct: Look at Table 1. The full-length construct is 100. With the enhancer in the reverse orientation, activity is 95. With the enhancer moved 3 kb downstream of the reporter, it is 90. Compare that to enhancer deleted at 12. So the enhancer still works nearly as well when it is flipped or placed on the other side of the gene. Working in any orientation and from a distance, upstream or downstream, is a hallmark of enhancers. A promoter, by contrast, must be in the right place and the right direction. Why the others are wrong: moving the enhancer doesn't turn it into a promoter, since it doesn't supply a TATA box and activity stays about the same; working only upstream and forward is contradicted by 95 and 90; needing to sit next to the TATA box is contradicted by the enhancer working from 1,200 bp upstream and even from 3 kb downstream. Trap: Applying the strict position and orientation rules of a promoter to an enhancer.

qs.q: The near-complete loss of activity when the TATA box is deleted indicates that the TATA box is needed for:
o: assembly of the general transcription factors, including TBP, that position RNA polymerase II at the start site
Correct: TBP binds the TATA box and starts assembly of the factors that position RNA polymerase II at the start site.
splicing of the reporter transcript
Not quite. Splicing happens after transcription, so it wouldn't cut transcript production this much.
binding of the activating transcription factor at the enhancer
Not quite. The enhancer binds the activator, and enhancer deletion only lowered activity to 12.
translation of luciferase mRNA by ribosomes
Not quite. The TATA box is a DNA element, not something ribosomes read.
qs.x: Correct: Table 1 shows deleting the TATA box drops activity to 3, close to the promoterless vector at 1. The TATA box is a short DNA sequence in the core promoter, which in the passage sits 30 bp upstream of the start site (paragraph 1). A protein called TBP (part of the general factor TFIID) binds it. That starts the assembly of the other general transcription factors, which put RNA polymerase II in the right place to start copying. Without the TATA box, that complex can't be built, so basal transcription (the baseline level) fails. Why the others are wrong: splicing happens after transcription, so it wouldn't cut transcript production this much; the enhancer binds the activator (paragraph 2), not the TATA box, and removing the enhancer only drops activity to 12; the TATA box is a DNA element, and ribosomes read mRNA, not this DNA. Trap: Assigning the TATA box a role in steps after transcription instead of initiation.

qs.q: Co-transfection with the Renilla luciferase plasmid is used to:
o: identify the transcription factor bound to the enhancer
Not quite. The Renilla plasmid says nothing about which transcription factor binds the enhancer.
correct for transfection differences
Correct: Dividing by the constitutive Renilla signal corrects for plasmid uptake and cell number.
increase the expression of firefly luciferase
Not quite. Renilla is a separate reporter and doesn't boost firefly expression.
measure the rate of mRNA degradation of the reporter
Not quite. The ratio reports relative activity, not mRNA decay.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says each reporter plasmid was transfected together with a second plasmid that constitutively expresses Renilla luciferase (it is always on, at a steady level). Different dishes may have taken up different amounts of plasmid, or had different numbers of living cells. Renilla would vary with those same factors, but the construct being tested doesn't affect it. By dividing firefly activity by Renilla activity, as the passage says was done, those differences cancel. What's left reflects the effect of the construct. That is why this works as an internal control. Why the others are wrong: Renilla carries no information about which transcription factor binds the enhancer; it is a separate reporter and doesn't increase firefly expression; the ratio reports relative activity, not the rate of mRNA decay. Trap: Assuming the second reporter measures the biology under study, when it only normalizes.

r: Enhancer moved 3 kb downstream of reporter

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: A laboratory colony of 500 flour beetles was used to study the evolution of resistance to an insecticide. Resistance is controlled by a single autosomal locus: allele R is completely dominant to allele r, so RR and Rr beetles survive exposure and rr beetles are susceptible. Beetles in generation 0 were genotyped before any exposure, and the counts are shown in Table 1. The colony mated randomly. In every generation, adult beetles were exposed to the insecticide, and 100% of RR, 100% of Rr, and 20% of rr beetles survived to reproduce. The survivors were then allowed to mate at random to produce the next generation, which was again exposed. The calculated frequency of allele R at the start of each generation is plotted in Figure 1.
Assume that the population is large, that there is no mutation or migration, and that selection is the only factor changing allele frequencies.

qs.q: What is the frequency of allele R in generation 0?
o: Not quite. 0.36 is the fraction of beetles carrying at least one R, not the allele frequency.
Not quite. 0.04 is the frequency of RR beetles, 20 ÷ 500.
Correct: R alleles = 2(20) + 160 = 200 out of 1,000 alleles, so p = 0.20.
Not quite. 0.32 is the heterozygote frequency, 160 ÷ 500.
qs.x: Correct: Allele frequency is the fraction of all gene copies that are R. Formula: p = (number of R alleles) ÷ (total alleles). Each beetle has 2 alleles at this locus. Table 1: RR = 20, Rr = 160, rr = 320. Total beetles = 20 + 160 + 320 = 500, so total alleles = 2 × 500 = 1,000. R alleles: each RR beetle has 2, each Rr has 1. So 2 × 20 + 160 = 40 + 160 = 200. Plug in: p = 200 ÷ 1,000 = 0.20. This agrees with Figure 1, which starts at 0.2 in generation 0. Why the others are wrong: 0.36 is the fraction of beetles with at least one R, (20 + 160) ÷ 500 = 0.36, which is a phenotype fraction, not an allele frequency; 0.04 is RR beetles only, 20 ÷ 500; 0.32 is Rr beetles only, 160 ÷ 500. Trap: Using the fraction of resistant beetles, or the heterozygote frequency, as the allele frequency.

qs.q: After the first exposure, the frequency of allele R among the surviving parents is closest to:
o: Not quite. 0.36 is the fraction of beetles carrying R before selection, not the allele frequency among survivors.
Not quite. That would need equal numbers of R and r alleles among survivors, which the counts don't give.
Not quite. 0.20 is the frequency before selection.
Correct: Survivors are 20 RR, 160 Rr and 64 rr, so p = 200 ÷ 488 = 0.41.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says all RR and Rr beetles survive, and only 20% of rr beetles survive. Survivors: RR = 20 (100% of 20). Rr = 160 (100% of 160). rr = 20% of 320 = 0.20 × 320 = 64. Total survivors = 20 + 160 + 64 = 244, which means 2 × 244 = 488 alleles. R alleles among survivors = 2 × 20 + 160 = 200. Plug in: p = 200 ÷ 488 = 0.41. That matches Figure 1, where generation 1 is 0.41. The number of R copies stayed at 200, but the total alleles dropped from 1,000 to 488, so R is a bigger share. Why the others are wrong: 0.36 is the fraction of beetles with R before selection; 0.50 would need equal numbers of R and r alleles, which the counts don't give; 0.20 is the frequency before selection, which didn't take into account the loss of rr beetles. Trap: Forgetting to recount the total alleles after the susceptible beetles are removed.

qs.q: In Figure 1, the increase in the frequency of R per generation becomes smaller as R becomes common. The best explanation is that:
o: mutation from R to r increasingly offsets the effect of selection
Not quite. The passage says there is no mutation.
as allele r becomes rare, most r copies reside in Rr beetles that survive, so selection removes fewer r alleles each generation
Correct: When r is rare, most r copies hide in surviving Rr beetles, so selection removes fewer each generation.
genetic drift is strongest when an allele is common in a large population
Not quite. Drift is weak in large populations, and the passage assumes none.
the insecticide becomes less toxic to rr beetles as generations pass
Not quite. rr survival was fixed at 20% in every generation.
qs.x: Correct: Figure 1 shows R going 0.20, 0.41, 0.568, 0.668, 0.732, 0.777, 0.809. The gains each generation are about 0.21, 0.16, 0.10, 0.06, 0.05 and 0.03, so they keep shrinking. Selection here works only against rr beetles, because RR and Rr survive equally (paragraph 1, where R is completely dominant). When r is common, there are many rr beetles for selection to remove. When r becomes rare, almost all r copies sit in Rr beetles, which survive. Few r copies are removed per generation, so the allele frequency changes more slowly. Why the others are wrong: the passage rules out mutation (paragraph 2); genetic drift is weak in large populations, and the passage assumes only selection acts; rr survival was fixed at 20% in every generation, so the insecticide's toxicity didn't change. Trap: Expecting a constant gain per generation and blaming forces that the passage rules out.

qs.q: Which mode of natural selection is operating on the resistance trait in this experiment?
o: Directional selection, favoring one extreme
Correct: Allele frequency moves steadily one way because the resistant phenotype is favored.
Sexual selection, because beetles choose mates by phenotype
Not quite. Mating was random, and survival, not mate choice, drives the change.
Stabilizing selection, because intermediate genotypes are favored
Not quite. Rr isn't favored over RR. Resistant phenotypes are equally fit.
Disruptive selection, because both extremes are favored
Not quite. Only one extreme, resistance, has an advantage.
qs.x: Correct: There are three main modes of selection. Directional selection favors one extreme and pushes allele frequency in one direction. Stabilizing selection favors the middle and disfavors both extremes. Disruptive selection favors both extremes over the middle. Here, resistant beetles (RR and Rr) survive 100% and susceptible beetles (rr) survive only 20% (paragraph 1). Only one phenotype is favored over the other, and Figure 1 shows R rising steadily from 0.2 to 0.809. That is directional selection. Why the others are wrong: sexual selection is about mate choice, but paragraph 1 says mating was random; stabilizing selection would favor intermediate genotypes, but Rr is no better than RR; disruptive selection would favor both extremes, but only one extreme, resistance, has an advantage. Trap: Picking stabilizing selection because the heterozygote shows the dominant phenotype.

qs.q: Suppose the insecticide is withdrawn after generation 6, and R carriers have lower fertility than rr beetles. The frequency of R is most likely to:
o: decline over subsequent generations, because carriers of R now have lower reproductive fitness
Correct: Without the insecticide, the fertility cost of R becomes the main selective force, so R frequency falls.
drop to zero in a single generation
Not quite. R persists in heterozygotes, so it can't disappear in one generation.
increase further, because dominant alleles always increase in frequency
Not quite. Dominance doesn't decide the direction of selection. Fitness does.
remain at 0.81, because allele frequencies at Hardy-Weinberg proportions never change under any conditions
Not quite. Hardy-Weinberg stability needs no selection, and a fertility cost is selection.
qs.x: Correct: In the experiment, R spread because the insecticide killed most rr beetles (paragraph 1). If the insecticide is withdrawn, that benefit disappears. The question adds that R carriers have lower fertility than rr beetles. Now beetles with R have fewer offspring than rr beetles, so selection favors r. Each generation, R passes to fewer offspring than r, so the frequency of R falls over time. It can't vanish in one step, because R still hides in Rr beetles, and r beetles gain only a modest edge. Why the others are wrong: dropping to zero in one generation is too fast, since carriers still reproduce; increasing because dominant alleles always spread is false, because dominance doesn't set the direction of selection, fitness does; staying at 0.81 forever treats Hardy-Weinberg as always true, but it needs no selection, and a fertility cost is selection. Trap: Assuming dominant alleles are favored automatically and ignoring fitness costs.
