passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: In maize, kernel color is controlled by a gene with alleles P (purple, dominant) and p (yellow), and kernel starch type is controlled by a gene with alleles W (starchy, dominant) and w (waxy). A plant that was heterozygous at both genes was crossed to a plant that was homozygous recessive at both genes (a testcross). The heterozygous parent was the progeny of a cross between a purple, starchy line and a yellow, waxy line. A total of 1,000 kernels from the testcross were scored for color and starch type, and the results are listed in Table 1.

A geneticist who also wished to place a third gene, X, on the same chromosome carried out similar testcrosses and found that recombinant kernels between X and the color gene made up 5% of progeny, whereas recombinant kernels between X and the starch gene made up 17% of progeny. Both genes studied here are on the same chromosome pair, and no double crossovers were detected.

qs.q: The testcross results are most consistent with which conclusion?
o: The genes assort independently, because all four phenotypes appear
Not quite. Linked genes also give all four classes. Independent assortment needs equal numbers.
The yellow and waxy alleles are dominant, because the testcross parent was homozygous recessive
Not quite. The recessive parent shows its alleles are recessive. It doesn't make yellow or waxy dominant.
The color and starch genes are linked, because the parental phenotypes are far more frequent than the recombinant phenotypes
Correct: The parental classes (440 and 440) far outnumber the recombinants (60 and 60), which shows linkage.
The genes are on different chromosomes, because recombinants are observed
Not quite. Recombinants also occur for linked genes, through crossing over.
qs.x: Correct: A testcross crosses a double heterozygote with a double recessive. If the two genes sorted independently (on different chromosomes or far apart), the four kernel types would come out about equal, 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, so 250 each out of 1,000. Table 1 shows 440, 60, 60 and 440. Two classes (purple starchy and yellow waxy) are far more common than the other two. That means the alleles tend to travel together on the same chromosome: the genes are linked. The rare classes are recombinants from crossing over. Why the others are wrong: seeing all four phenotypes doesn't prove independent assortment, since linked genes make recombinants too, and independence needs equal numbers; the homozygous recessive parent shows that its alleles are recessive and says nothing about dominance of yellow or waxy; recombinants appear for linked genes through crossing over, so seeing them doesn't mean different chromosomes (and paragraph 2 says both genes are on the same chromosome pair). Trap: Reading all four classes being present as evidence of independent assortment.

qs.q: What is the map distance between the color gene and the starch gene?
o: 50 map units
Not quite. 50 is the maximum recombination frequency, seen for unlinked genes.
88 map units
Not quite. 88 is the percent of parental kernels, not recombinants.
6 map units
Not quite. 6 counts only one recombinant class.
12 map units
Correct: Recombinants are 60 + 60 = 120 out of 1,000, which is 12% or 12 map units.
qs.x: Correct: Map distance in map units (centimorgans) equals the recombination frequency as a percent. Formula: recombination frequency = (recombinant kernels) ÷ (total kernels). The recombinants are the rare classes in Table 1: purple waxy (60) and yellow starchy (60). Recombinants = 60 + 60 = 120. Total = 440 + 60 + 60 + 440 = 1,000. Plug in: 120 ÷ 1,000 = 0.12 = 12%. 1% recombination is 1 map unit, so the distance is 12 map units. Why the others are wrong: 50 is the maximum recombination frequency, which unlinked genes show; 88 is the percent of parental kernels, (440 + 440) ÷ 1,000; 6 counts only one recombinant class (60 ÷ 1,000 = 6%). Trap: Counting only one of the two recombinant classes, or reporting the parental percentage.

qs.q: Which genotype arrangement did the heterozygous parent carry?
o: P w on one chromosome and p W on the homologous chromosome
Not quite. That arrangement would make purple waxy and yellow starchy the most common classes.
P W on both chromosomes
Not quite. The parent was heterozygous at both genes, so it can't be P W on both.
p w on both chromosomes
Not quite. p w on both chromosomes wouldn't be heterozygous and would give only yellow waxy kernels.
P W on one chromosome and p w on the homologous chromosome
Correct: Purple starchy and yellow waxy are the common parental classes, so P travels with W and p with w.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says the heterozygous parent came from a cross of a purple, starchy line with a yellow, waxy line. That would give a plant with P and W from one parent on one chromosome, and p and w from the other parent on the other chromosome. That is called the cis (coupling) arrangement. The testcross data confirm it. The parent's gametes decide the offspring phenotypes (the testcross parent only gives p w). The most common classes in Table 1 are parental: purple starchy (440) and yellow waxy (440). So P travels with W, and p travels with w. Why the others are wrong: P w on one chromosome and p W on the other would make purple waxy and yellow starchy the common classes, but those are the rare ones (60 each); P W on both chromosomes would not be heterozygous; p w on both would also not be heterozygous, and would make only yellow waxy. Trap: Reading the arrangement off the rare recombinant classes instead of the common parental ones.

qs.q: Recombinant kernels arise from crossing over, which occurs:
o: between sister chromatids during prophase of mitosis
Not quite. Sister chromatids are identical, so exchange between them makes no new combinations.
between nonhomologous chromosomes during anaphase I
Not quite. Homologs separate in anaphase I. Exchange happens earlier, between paired homologs.
during prophase I of meiosis
Correct: Homologs pair in prophase I and nonsister chromatids in the tetrad swap segments.
between the two strands of DNA during S phase
Not quite. Replication copies DNA but doesn't exchange alleles between homologs.
qs.x: Correct: Crossing over is the swapping of pieces between two chromosomes, and it creates new combinations of alleles. In prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair up tightly (synapsis) to form a tetrad (four chromatids side by side). Nonsister chromatids, which belong to different homologs, trade segments. That is how the rare purple waxy and yellow starchy kernels (the recombinants in Table 1) get made. Why the others are wrong: sister chromatids are identical copies, so exchanging pieces between them makes no new allele combinations, and mitosis isn't how gametes are made; in anaphase I, homologs are pulled apart, and exchange happens earlier while they are paired; S phase copies DNA, but copying doesn't swap alleles between homologs. Trap: Placing crossing over in mitosis or during chromosome separation instead of when homologs pair.

qs.q: Given the recombination frequencies for gene X, the most likely order of the three genes is:
o: color gene, X, starch gene
Not quite. That order would make the X distances add up to 12, not 5 and 17.
color gene, starch gene, X
Not quite. That would put X closer to the starch gene, but X is farther from it.
X, starch gene, color gene
Not quite. That order would swap the distances, with X to starch 5 and X to color 17.
X, color gene, starch gene
Correct: X is 5 from color and 17 from starch, and 5 + 12 = 17, so color lies between X and starch.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says X is 5% recombinant with the color gene and 17% with the starch gene. So X is 5 map units from color and 17 from starch. The color and starch genes are 12 map units apart, from the earlier question. Map distances add up along a line. Try the order X, color, starch: X to color 5, plus color to starch 12, equals 5 + 12 = 17, which equals the distance X to starch. It fits. So the color gene is in the middle. Why the others are wrong: color, X, starch would make the X distances add to the color-starch distance, 12, but 5 and 17 don't; color, starch, X would put X closer to starch than to color, but X is farther from starch (17 versus 5); X, starch, color would swap the distances (X to starch 5, X to color 17), the reverse of the data. Trap: Ignoring that map distances add when ordering three linked genes.

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: A biochemist examined how cells drive thermodynamically unfavorable phosphorylation reactions by coupling them to reactions that release free energy. Standard free-energy changes at pH 7 (ΔG°') for several reactions are listed in Table 1. In the cell, reaction directions are determined by the actual free-energy change, ΔG = ΔG°' + RT ln Q, where Q is the reaction quotient. For these calculations the temperature is 310 K, and RT is about 2.6 kJ/mol. The biochemist also measured the concentrations of ATP, ADP, and inorganic phosphate (Pi) in a resting muscle cell and found that the ratio [ATP]/([ADP][Pi]) is maintained far above the value at equilibrium for ATP hydrolysis.

Glucose phosphorylation by hexokinase can be written as the sum of glucose + Pi giving glucose 6-phosphate (G6P) + H₂O, and ATP hydrolysis. Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) transfers its phosphoryl group to ADP in the final step of glycolysis, a reaction that generates ATP even though no oxygen is consumed directly in the step.

qs.q: What is the ΔG°' of the hexokinase reaction, glucose + ATP → G6P + ADP?
o: −44.3 kJ/mol
Not quite. This adds the magnitudes of both values and treats the phosphorylation as favorable.
+13.8 kJ/mol
Not quite. +13.8 ignores the ATP hydrolysis that drives the reaction.
+44.3 kJ/mol
Not quite. This adds the magnitudes as positive and gets the sign of the ATP term wrong.
−16.7 kJ/mol
qs.x: Correct: When two reactions are coupled, you add the reactions and add their ΔG°′ values. Paragraph 2 says the hexokinase reaction is the sum of glucose + Pi → G6P + H₂O and ATP hydrolysis. From Table 1: glucose + Pi → G6P + H₂O is +13.8 kJ/mol, and ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pi is −30.5 kJ/mol. Add the reactions. Pi appears on both sides and H₂O appears on both sides, so they cancel, leaving glucose + ATP → G6P + ADP. Add the numbers: +13.8 + (−30.5) = 13.8 − 30.5 = −16.7 kJ/mol. The sum is negative, so the coupled reaction is favorable. Why the others are wrong: −44.3 adds the magnitudes (13.8 + 30.5) and makes both negative; +13.8 is the phosphorylation alone, ignoring ATP hydrolysis; +44.3 adds the magnitudes as positives, which gets the sign of the ATP term wrong. Trap: Using the phosphorylation value alone instead of summing it with the ATP hydrolysis value.

qs.q: Why is the actual free energy released by ATP hydrolysis in the cell more negative than the standard value?
o: Because enzymes lower ΔG°' for ATP hydrolysis
Not quite. Enzymes change rates, not the free-energy change of a reaction.
Because ATP is converted to a more stable molecule before hydrolysis
Not quite. No such conversion occurs. The difference comes from concentrations in ΔG.
Because the cell raises the temperature to about 310 K
Not quite. Temperature isn't the cause. The difference comes from the ratio of ATP to its products.
Because the ratio [ATP]/([ADP][Pi]) is maintained far above its equilibrium value, the reaction quotient Q for hydrolysis is small
Correct: The cell keeps ATP high relative to ADP and Pi, so Q is small, ln Q is very negative and ΔG is more negative.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 gives the formula ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q. Here Q is the reaction quotient for hydrolysis: [ADP][Pi] ÷ [ATP]. Paragraph 1 also says the cell keeps [ATP] ÷ ([ADP][Pi]) far above its equilibrium value. That makes Q (the inverse of that ratio) very small, much smaller than at equilibrium. The natural log of a small number is a big negative number (ln of a number below 1 is negative). So RT ln Q is negative and adds to ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ/mol, making ΔG more negative than −30.5. The cell keeps ATP high compared to its products, which stores energy. Why the others are wrong: enzymes change the rate of a reaction and not its free-energy change, so they can't alter ΔG; ATP isn't converted to a more stable molecule before hydrolysis, and the difference comes from concentrations in ΔG; the standard value is already given at 310 K in paragraph 1 and small temperature effects don't explain it. Trap: Believing an enzyme can change a reaction's thermodynamics rather than just its speed.

qs.q: PEP can drive the formation of ATP from ADP because:
o: PEP and ATP have identical ΔG°' values, so the reaction is at equilibrium
Not quite. The two values differ by about 31 kJ/mol.
hydrolysis of PEP releases more free energy than ATP hydrolysis, giving PEP a higher phosphoryl transfer potential
Correct: PEP's −61.9 is more negative than ATP's −30.5, so passing its phosphate to ADP is favorable (net −31.4).
the reaction is driven by loss of pyruvate to the extracellular space
Not quite. Nothing in the data says pyruvate leaves the cell. The energetics come from the transfer values.
ATP has a higher phosphoryl transfer potential than PEP
Not quite. The data show PEP has the higher potential, so ATP to PEP is unfavorable.
qs.x: Correct: A molecule with a more negative ΔG°′ of hydrolysis has a higher phosphoryl transfer potential, meaning it hands off its phosphate group more readily. From Table 1, PEP + H₂O → pyruvate + Pi is −61.9 kJ/mol, and ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pi is −30.5 kJ/mol. Moving PEP's phosphate onto ADP means PEP hydrolysis (−61.9) plus ADP + Pi → ATP (the reverse of ATP hydrolysis, +30.5). Add: −61.9 + 30.5 = −31.4 kJ/mol. That is negative, so the transfer is favorable and ATP forms. Why the others are wrong: the values aren't equal; they differ by 61.9 − 30.5 = 31.4 kJ/mol; nothing in the data says pyruvate leaves the cell, and the energetics come from the group transfer values; ATP has a lower, not higher, phosphoryl transfer potential than PEP, so ATP-to-PEP transfer would be unfavorable. Trap: Assuming the energy currency (ATP) must have the highest phosphoryl transfer potential.

qs.q: At 310 K, the equilibrium constant for the isomerization G6P to F6P is closest to:
o: Not quite. 0.05 would need a ΔG°′ of about +7.8 kJ/mol.
Not quite. This drops the minus sign. A positive ΔG°′ favors the reactant.
Correct: Keq = e to the power of (−1.7 ÷ 2.6) = e to the power of −0.65 ≈ 0.5.
Not quite. 5 would need a ΔG°′ of about −4.2 kJ/mol.
qs.x: Correct: The link between ΔG°′ and the equilibrium constant is ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq, which rearranges to Keq = e raised to the power of (−ΔG°′ ÷ RT). Values: ΔG°′ for G6P → F6P is +1.7 kJ/mol (Table 1), RT = 2.6 kJ/mol (paragraph 1). Plug in: Keq = e to the power of (−1.7 ÷ 2.6). Divide: 1.7 ÷ 2.6 = 0.65, so the exponent is −0.65. e to the power of −0.65 is about 0.52, which is closest to 0.5. As a check, a positive ΔG°′ means the reaction is not favorable as written, so Keq should be below 1, and 0.5 is. Why the others are wrong: 0.05 would need a ΔG°′ of about +7.8 kJ/mol (0.05 = e⁻³, and 3 × 2.6 = 7.8); 2 drops the minus sign, since e to the power of +0.65 is about 1.9; 5 would need ΔG°′ of about −4.2 kJ/mol (5 = e¹·⁶, and 1.6 × 2.6 = 4.2). Trap: Dropping the minus sign in Keq = e to the power of (−ΔG°′ ÷ RT) and predicting that products are favored.

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: 10 endurance-trained and 10 untrained adults performed a graded exercise test on a cycle ergometer. Intensity was increased stepwise and is expressed as a percentage of each person's maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max). Blood lactate concentration was measured at the end of each stage; mean values are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. The lactate threshold is the intensity above which blood lactate begins to rise steeply. In a separate analysis, muscle biopsies were taken from the thigh at rest, and the activity of citrate synthase, a mitochondrial matrix enzyme of the citric acid cycle that is used as an indicator of mitochondrial content, was measured. Mean citrate synthase activity was 42 µmol/min per gram of tissue in trained subjects and 20 µmol/min per gram in untrained subjects.

During intense exercise, muscle releases lactate into the blood. The liver takes up lactate from the blood. All subjects fasted overnight, avoided strenuous exercise for 48 hours beforehand, and were tested at the same time of day.

qs.q: At 70% VO2max, the blood lactate concentration in untrained subjects compared with trained subjects is about:
o: 2 times lower
Not quite. Untrained subjects have more lactate, so the ratio is above 1.
the same
Not quite. The groups differ at 70%, 2.8 mM versus 1.3 mM.
4 times higher
Not quite. 4 times higher would need untrained lactate near 5.2 mM.
2 times higher
Correct: 2.8 ÷ 1.3 is about 2.2, so untrained lactate is roughly double.
qs.x: Correct: Read the 70% row of Table 1: untrained lactate is 2.8 mM and trained lactate is 1.3 mM. The question asks untrained compared with trained, so divide untrained by trained: 2.8 ÷ 1.3. 1.3 × 2 = 2.6, which is just under 2.8, so the answer is a little over 2. More exactly, 2.8 ÷ 1.3 = 2.15, so about 2.2 at most, close to 2. Untrained subjects have about twice the lactate. Why the others are wrong: 2 times lower flips the ratio, since untrained lactate is higher, so the ratio is above 1; the same isn't true, because the groups differ (2.8 versus 1.3 mM); 4 times higher would need untrained lactate near 5.2 mM (4 × 1.3). Trap: Subtracting (2.8 − 1.3 = 1.5 mM) and then treating that as a ratio.

qs.q: The conversion of pyruvate to lactate during intense exercise is metabolically important because it:
o: converts NAD⁺ to NADH to feed the electron transport chain
Not quite. The reaction runs the other way, consuming NADH to make NAD⁺.
regenerates NAD⁺ for glycolysis
Correct: LDH oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, which glycolysis needs to keep running.
generates additional ATP through substrate-level phosphorylation
Not quite. The LDH step makes no ATP. Its benefit is regenerating NAD⁺.
synthesizes glucose directly within muscle
Not quite. Muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase and doesn't make free glucose from lactate.
qs.x: Correct: Glycolysis turns glucose into pyruvate. One step, done by glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase, needs NAD⁺ and turns it into NADH. Glycolysis can't keep running unless NAD⁺ is made again. In intense exercise, mitochondria (and oxygen) can't keep up. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) fixes this by turning pyruvate into lactate while oxidizing NADH to NAD⁺. The recycled NAD⁺ lets glycolysis continue and keep making ATP. Why the others are wrong: the reaction doesn't convert NAD⁺ to NADH, it does the opposite and uses up NADH; the LDH step makes no ATP, and ATP comes from other steps of glycolysis; muscle can't make free glucose from lactate, because it lacks glucose 6-phosphatase. Trap: Thinking lactate formation makes ATP, when it only regenerates NAD⁺.

qs.q: Higher citrate synthase activity in trained muscle most likely contributes to the higher lactate threshold because:
o: citrate synthase converts lactate directly to glucose
Not quite. Citrate synthase joins acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate. It doesn't act on lactate.
mitochondria in trained subjects produce lactate at a lower rate because they lack NADH
Not quite. Mitochondria use NADH. The difference comes from greater oxidative capacity.
greater mitochondrial content allows more pyruvate to be oxidized aerobically, reducing reliance on lactate formation
Correct: More mitochondria oxidize more pyruvate aerobically, so less is diverted to lactate.
citrate synthase is a glycolytic enzyme that speeds lactate production
Not quite. Citrate synthase is a citric acid cycle enzyme in the matrix.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says citrate synthase is a mitochondrial matrix enzyme of the citric acid cycle, used as a marker of mitochondrial content. Trained muscle has 42 µmol/min per gram, versus 20 for untrained. That is 42 ÷ 20 = 2.1, so about twice the mitochondria. More mitochondria means more capacity to burn pyruvate with oxygen (aerobic oxidation). At the same exercise intensity, less pyruvate is left over to be turned into lactate. That is why trained subjects stay at lower lactate (Table 1 shows 1.3 mM versus 2.8 mM at 70% VO2max) and have a higher lactate threshold. Why the others are wrong: citrate synthase joins acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate and doesn't act on lactate or make glucose; mitochondria use NADH, so trained cells don't make less lactate because they lack it; citrate synthase is a citric acid cycle enzyme in the matrix, not a glycolytic one. Trap: Giving citrate synthase a glycolytic role when it is just a marker of mitochondrial content.

qs.q: In the liver, lactate taken up from the blood is mainly:
o: stored directly as lactate in glycogen granules
Not quite. Glycogen is a polymer of glucose, not lactate.
made into glucose and released into blood
Correct: In the Cori cycle the liver turns lactate into pyruvate and then glucose, which goes back to the blood.
excreted unchanged in the bile through the biliary ducts
Not quite. Bile isn't a route for lactate disposal.
converted to fatty acids that are exported as chylomicrons
Not quite. Chylomicrons come from intestinal cells and dietary fat, not liver lactate.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 2 says muscle releases lactate into the blood during intense exercise and the liver takes it up. In the liver, lactate dehydrogenase turns lactate back into pyruvate. The liver then runs gluconeogenesis (making glucose from non-sugar starting materials) and makes glucose, which it releases into the blood. Muscle can take that glucose up again. This loop is the Cori cycle. Why the others are wrong: glycogen is a polymer of glucose units, and lactate isn't stored directly in it; bile is not a route for lactate disposal; chylomicrons are made in intestinal cells from dietary fat, and lactate isn't sent this way. Trap: Mixing up the liver's glucose-making fate for lactate with lipid export.

qs.q: Between 85% and 100% VO2max, how does the rise in lactate in trained subjects compare with that in untrained subjects?
o: It is larger in trained subjects, 6.0 mM compared with 4.5 mM
Correct: Trained rise is 9.0 − 3.0 = 6.0 mM, untrained is 11.0 − 6.5 = 4.5 mM.
It is larger in untrained subjects, because their final lactate is higher
Not quite. The final value is higher in untrained subjects, but the question asks about the rise from the 85% value.
It is smaller in trained subjects, 1.5 mM compared with 4.5 mM
Not quite. 1.5 mM isn't the rise for either group, and trained subjects rose more.
It is the same in both groups, 4.5 mM
Not quite. Only the untrained subjects rise 4.5 mM. Trained subjects rise 6.0 mM.
qs.x: Correct: The rise between two stages is the 100% value minus the 85% value, from Table 1. Trained: 9.0 − 3.0 = 6.0 mM. Untrained: 11.0 − 6.5 = 4.5 mM. Since 6.0 is bigger than 4.5, the rise is larger in trained subjects. It happens because the trained group starts from a much lower lactate at 85% (3.0 versus 6.5), so there is more room to rise, and by 100% they have passed their lactate threshold. Why the others are wrong: untrained subjects do have the higher final value (11.0 versus 9.0), but the question asks about the rise between stages; 1.5 mM isn't the rise for either group (it's about 11.0 − 9.0 = 2.0 or 6.0 − 4.5 = 1.5, a difference of the rises); both groups rising 4.5 mM is true only for the untrained group. Trap: Comparing the endpoint values at 100% instead of the change between two stages.

questions.q: Which amino acid is most likely to disrupt an α helix when it appears in the middle of the helix?
o: Alanine
Not quite. Alanine has a small methyl side chain and is a strong helix-former.
Leucine
Not quite. Leucine is common in helices and fits easily.
Proline
Correct: Proline's side chain bonds to its backbone nitrogen, which leaves no amide hydrogen for bonding and restricts rotation, so it kinks the helix.
Glutamate
Not quite. Glutamate readily occurs in helices, even though its charge can interact with neighboring side chains.
questions.x: Correct: An α helix is held together by hydrogen bonds along the backbone. The N–H of each amide group bonds to a C=O four residues earlier. Proline breaks this in two ways. Its side chain loops back and bonds to its own backbone nitrogen, so that nitrogen has no hydrogen left to donate in a hydrogen bond. The ring also locks the backbone angle, so the chain can't twist into the regular helix shape. In the middle of a helix, proline puts in a kink. Why the others are wrong: alanine has a small methyl side chain and is one of the best helix-formers; leucine is common in helices and fits easily; glutamate readily appears in helices, though its charge can interact with neighboring side chains. Trap: Picking the largest or most polar side chain, when what matters is whether the residue can join the backbone hydrogen bonds.

questions.q: Which feature of a eukaryotic mRNA primarily protects its 5' end from degradation by exonucleases?
o: A Shine-Dalgarno sequence
Not quite. A Shine-Dalgarno sequence is a ribosome binding site in prokaryotic mRNA.
A 7-methylguanosine cap
Correct: The 5' 7-methylguanosine cap blocks 5'-to-3' exonuclease attack and helps ribosome binding.
Removal of introns by spliceosomes
Not quite. Splicing removes introns but doesn't protect the 5' end from exonucleases.
A poly-A tail
Not quite. The poly-A tail protects the 3' end, not the 5' end.
questions.x: Correct: Exonucleases are enzymes that chew a nucleic acid from its ends. A eukaryotic mRNA needs protection on both ends. At the 5' end, that's the 7-methylguanosine cap, a modified guanine added backward to the first nucleotide as the RNA is still being made. It blocks 5'-to-3' exonucleases from starting at the end, and it also helps the ribosome bind to start translation. Why the others are wrong: a Shine-Dalgarno sequence is the ribosome binding site on prokaryotic mRNA and isn't found in eukaryotic mRNA; splicing removes introns but doesn't shield the 5' end; the poly-A tail protects the 3' end, not the 5' end. Trap: Picking the poly-A tail, which guards the opposite end of the transcript.

questions.q: A woman who carries one copy of the X-linked recessive allele for red-green color blindness has children with a man with normal color vision. What is the probability that a daughter of this couple will be color blind?
o: Not quite. 1/4 applies the autosomal recessive ratio, which doesn't fit an X-linked trait with a normal father.
Not quite. A probability of 1 would require the father to be affected as well.
Not quite. 1/2 is the chance a son is affected, not a daughter.
Correct: The father passes every daughter a normal X, so daughters can be carriers but never color blind.
questions.x: Correct: Red-green color blindness is X-linked recessive. Call the normal X allele X and the color-blind allele Xᶜ. Mother is a carrier, so XXᶜ. Father has normal color vision, so XY. A daughter always gets one X from each parent. The father can only give his X, which is normal. So every daughter is either XX (normal) or XXᶜ (a carrier with normal vision). To be color blind a daughter would need XᶜXᶜ, and that needs an Xᶜ from the father, who doesn't have one. So the probability is 0. Why the others are wrong: 1/4 uses the autosomal recessive ratio, which doesn't fit an X-linked trait with a normal father; 1 would require the father to be affected too; 1/2 is the chance a son is color blind (a son gets the mother's X, which is Xᶜ half the time), not a daughter. Trap: Using the answer for sons when the question asks about daughters.

questions.q: In the citric acid cycle, which step produces a nucleoside triphosphate by substrate-level phosphorylation?
o: Isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate
Not quite. This oxidative decarboxylation reduces NAD⁺ to NADH. No GTP is made.
Succinate to fumarate
Not quite. This step reduces FAD to FADH₂ using a membrane-bound enzyme.
Succinyl-CoA to succinate
Correct: Succinyl-CoA synthetase uses the thioester bond energy to make GTP (or ATP) from GDP and Pi.
Malate to oxaloacetate
Not quite. This step reduces NAD⁺ to NADH and doesn't directly make a nucleoside triphosphate.
questions.x: Correct: Substrate-level phosphorylation means making a high-energy phosphate bond directly from a reaction, without using the electron transport chain. In the citric acid cycle that is one step. Succinyl-CoA has a high-energy thioester bond to coenzyme A. The enzyme succinyl-CoA synthetase breaks that bond to turn succinyl-CoA into succinate, and uses the released energy to join phosphate (Pi) onto GDP, making GTP (or ADP making ATP, depending on the tissue). Why the others are wrong: isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate is an oxidative decarboxylation that reduces NAD⁺ to NADH; succinate to fumarate reduces FAD to FADH₂ using a membrane-bound enzyme; malate to oxaloacetate reduces NAD⁺ to NADH and makes no nucleoside triphosphate directly. Trap: Choosing a step that makes NADH or FADH₂, which are oxidation steps and not direct phosphorylation.

questions.q: Hepatocytes of a patient taking a drug for many months show a marked expansion of an organelle that contains cytochrome P450 enzymes. Which organelle has expanded?
o: Peroxisome, a single-membrane organelle for oxidation
Not quite. Peroxisomes handle fatty acid oxidation and hydrogen peroxide, not P450 drug oxidation.
Rough endoplasmic reticulum studded with ribosomes
Not quite. Rough ER makes secreted and membrane proteins, not P450 drug detoxification.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Correct: The smooth ER holds P450 detoxification enzymes and expands with chronic drug exposure.
Golgi apparatus, the cisternal stack near the nucleus
Not quite. The Golgi modifies and sorts proteins and lipids. It isn't where drugs are metabolized.
questions.x: Correct: Cytochrome P450 enzymes oxidize drugs and other foreign chemicals to make them easier to get rid of. They sit in the membranes of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (smooth ER), the ER without ribosomes. The liver is the main detox organ. When a drug is taken for months, hepatocytes make more P450, and to hold it they expand the smooth ER membrane. This is a classic finding. Why the others are wrong: peroxisomes handle fatty acid oxidation and hydrogen peroxide, not P450 drug oxidation; rough ER, with ribosomes, makes secreted and membrane proteins; the Golgi apparatus modifies and sorts proteins and lipids and doesn't do drug metabolism. Trap: Choosing rough ER because it's the more familiar kind of ER.

questions.q: In bacterial conjugation between an F+ donor and an F- recipient, what is transferred, and what is the usual outcome?
o: One strand of the F plasmid passes through a pilus-formed bridge, and the recipient becomes F+
Correct: One strand of the F plasmid passes through the pilus bridge and is copied in both cells, so the recipient becomes F+.
The entire donor chromosome passes, and the recipient becomes an Hfr cell
Not quite. Only Hfr cells transfer chromosomal genes, and usually only part of the chromosome.
Phage particles carry donor DNA, and the recipient becomes lysogenic
Not quite. Phage carrying donor DNA is transduction, not conjugation.
Free DNA is taken up from the medium, and the recipient becomes antibiotic resistant
Not quite. Taking up free DNA from the medium is transformation, not conjugation.
questions.x: Correct: F+ cells carry the F plasmid, a small circle of DNA containing the genes to make a pilus, a thin tube. The F+ donor uses the pilus to grab an F- recipient and pull it close. A bridge forms, and one strand of the F plasmid is cut and passed through into the recipient. Then each cell makes a new complementary strand to match its single strand. Both end up with a complete F plasmid, so the recipient becomes F+. The donor keeps its copy too. Why the others are wrong: passing the whole donor chromosome and making an Hfr cell is wrong, because only Hfr cells (F factor integrated) transfer chromosomal genes, and usually only part of the chromosome; phage particles carrying donor DNA is transduction; taking up free DNA from the medium is transformation. Trap: Mixing up conjugation with transformation or transduction.

questions.q: A human cell has 46 chromosomes in G1. Which description applies to the same cell in G2?
o: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids
Correct: DNA is copied in S phase, so each of the 46 chromosomes has two sister chromatids, giving 92 chromatids.
92 chromosomes, 92 chromatids
Not quite. The chromosome count doesn't double until sister chromatids separate in anaphase.
23 chromosomes, 46 chromatids
Not quite. The cell stays diploid with 46 chromosomes. Halving happens after meiosis I.
46 chromosomes, 46 chromatids
Not quite. 46 chromatids is the G1 state, before replication.
questions.x: Correct: Count chromosomes by centromeres and count chromatids by DNA copies. In G1 the cell has 46 chromosomes, and each is a single piece of DNA (one chromatid). In S phase the DNA is replicated, so each chromosome now has two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere. The centromere count hasn't changed, so the cell still has 46 chromosomes. The chromatid count doubles: 46 × 2 = 92 chromatids. G2 comes after S, so a G2 cell has 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids. Why the others are wrong: 92 chromosomes would not happen until anaphase, when sister chromatids separate and each becomes its own chromosome; 23 chromosomes with 46 chromatids is half the number, which happens only after meiosis I; 46 chromosomes with 46 chromatids is the G1 state, before replication. Trap: Counting each chromatid as a chromosome after DNA replication.

questions.q: A toxin blocks voltage-gated potassium channels in a neuron but leaves voltage-gated sodium channels functional. Compared with a normal action potential, the action potential in the treated neuron will most likely:
o: have a larger hyperpolarization afterward
Not quite. The afterhyperpolarization depends on K⁺ efflux, so blocking K⁺ channels would shrink it.
have an increased resting membrane potential because K⁺ leaves faster
Not quite. The toxin lowers K⁺ permeability, so K⁺ leaves more slowly, not faster.
fail to depolarize
Not quite. Depolarization depends on Na⁺ influx through channels that still work.
have a prolonged repolarization phase
Correct: Outward K⁺ current drives repolarization. Without it, the membrane stays depolarized longer.
questions.x: Correct: An action potential has two main phases. First, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes in, which depolarizes the membrane (makes it more positive). Then the Na⁺ channels inactivate, and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, so K⁺ flows out. That outward K⁺ current is what brings the membrane back down, called repolarization. The toxin blocks the K⁺ channels but not the Na⁺ channels. So depolarization is normal, but the way back down is slow because the K⁺ exit is reduced. The membrane stays depolarized longer, and repolarization is prolonged. Why the others are wrong: a larger hyperpolarization afterward is wrong because that undershoot comes from K⁺ efflux and would be smaller; an increased resting membrane potential from faster K⁺ loss is wrong because the toxin slows, not speeds, K⁺ loss; failing to depolarize is wrong because depolarization depends on Na⁺ influx through channels that still work. Trap: Reversing the roles of Na⁺ and K⁺ channels in the phases of the action potential.

questions.q: In which segment of the nephron is the largest fraction of filtered water reabsorbed?
o: Collecting duct
Not quite. Water reabsorption in the collecting duct varies with ADH and is far less than in the proximal tubule.
Proximal convoluted tubule
Correct: About two-thirds of the filtered water follows active solute reabsorption in the proximal tubule.
Descending limb of the loop of Henle
Not quite. The descending limb reabsorbs a smaller amount, roughly 15% of filtered water.
Distal convoluted tubule
Not quite. The distal tubule reabsorbs a small fraction, which hormones adjust.
questions.x: Correct: Each day the kidney filters a huge volume of fluid into the nephron, and then takes most of it back. Most of it, about two-thirds, is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT). Here cells actively pump Na⁺ and other solutes (like glucose and amino acids) out of the filtrate, and water follows them by osmosis through many aquaporins. So about 67% of filtered water goes back in this first segment alone. Why the others are wrong: the collecting duct reabsorbs water under ADH control, but the amount is much smaller than in the proximal tubule; the descending limb of the loop of Henle takes back a smaller amount, roughly 15% of filtered water; the distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs a small fraction, fine-tuned by hormones. Trap: Picking the collecting duct because ADH regulates it, instead of the segment that handles the most volume.

questions.q: Which hormone acts by diffusing across the plasma membrane and binding to an intracellular receptor that regulates gene transcription?
o: Glucagon
Not quite. Glucagon acts through a cell-surface G protein-coupled receptor and cAMP.
Cortisol
Correct: Cortisol is a lipid-soluble steroid that enters the cell and binds an intracellular receptor that regulates transcription.
Epinephrine
Not quite. Epinephrine binds G protein-coupled receptors on the cell surface.
Insulin
Not quite. Insulin binds a receptor tyrosine kinase at the cell surface.
questions.x: Correct: Hormones signal in one of two ways. Water-soluble ones (peptides and most amines) can't cross the cell membrane, so they bind a receptor on the cell surface and start a second messenger cascade. Lipid-soluble ones (steroids, thyroid hormone) slip through the membrane, bind a receptor inside the cell, and the complex goes to the DNA to turn genes on or off, acting as a transcription factor. Cortisol is a steroid hormone made from cholesterol, so it follows the second route. Why the others are wrong: glucagon acts through a G protein-coupled receptor on the surface and raises cAMP; epinephrine also binds G protein-coupled receptors on the surface of target cells; insulin binds a receptor tyrosine kinase at the cell surface. Trap: Choosing a peptide or amine hormone, which signals from the cell surface.

questions.q: A decrease in blood pH, as occurs in exercising muscle, affects the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve in which way?
o: It does not shift, because hemoglobin responds only to PO₂
Not quite. Hemoglobin is also regulated by pH, CO₂, temperature and 2,3-BPG, not only PO₂.
It shifts to the right, lowering hemoglobin affinity for O₂ and promoting unloading of O₂ in tissues
Correct: The Bohr effect: acid and CO₂ stabilize the T state, so the curve shifts right and more O₂ is unloaded.
It shifts to the left, increasing hemoglobin affinity for O₂
Not quite. A leftward shift comes from alkalosis or lower temperature, not lower pH.
It becomes hyperbolic, because acid disrupts cooperativity
Not quite. The curve stays sigmoidal. Acid shifts it and doesn't remove cooperativity.
questions.x: Correct: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve plots how full hemoglobin is with O₂ against the O₂ pressure (PO₂). Exercising muscle makes extra CO₂ and lactic acid, which lowers pH. This is where the Bohr effect applies: extra H⁺ and CO₂ bind hemoglobin and stabilize its low-affinity (T) state. Hemoglobin then holds O₂ less tightly, so the curve shifts to the right. At a given PO₂, hemoglobin is less saturated, meaning more O₂ is released to the working muscle, which is exactly where it's needed. Why the others are wrong: no shift is wrong because hemoglobin is regulated by pH, CO₂, temperature and 2,3-BPG, not only PO₂; a leftward shift (higher affinity) comes from alkalosis or lower temperature; becoming hyperbolic is wrong because acid only shifts the curve and it stays sigmoidal. Trap: Shifting the curve left because lower pH seems like it should increase binding.

questions.q: Which statement describes facilitated diffusion of glucose through a GLUT transporter?
o: It is saturable and moves glucose down its concentration gradient without direct ATP use
Correct: GLUT transport is saturable, since carriers are limited, and moves glucose down its gradient without direct ATP use.
It is not saturable, because it depends on the lipid solubility of glucose
Not quite. Glucose isn't lipid soluble, and carrier-mediated transport saturates.
It requires a sodium gradient to couple glucose entry to sodium movement
Not quite. Coupling to sodium describes secondary active transport by SGLT proteins.
It moves glucose against its gradient using ATP hydrolysis
Not quite. Moving glucose against its gradient using ATP describes primary active transport.
questions.x: Correct: Facilitated diffusion is passive transport with a helper. Glucose is too big and polar to cross the lipid bilayer, so a GLUT carrier protein binds it on one side and releases it on the other. It moves glucose down its concentration gradient, from high to low, so the cell spends no ATP. But it needs a carrier, and there's a fixed number of carriers, so at high glucose they all get busy and the rate levels off (saturation). Why the others are wrong: saying it isn't saturable because of lipid solubility is wrong, since glucose isn't lipid soluble and carriers do saturate; needing a sodium gradient describes secondary active transport by SGLT proteins; moving against the gradient with ATP hydrolysis describes primary active transport. Trap: Mixing up carrier-mediated passive transport with active transport.
